short: A rapid share-price jump caused when firms that sold call options must keep buying the stock to protect themselves, pushing the price higher still.
kid: When lots of friends suddenly want the same sticker, the shopkeeper has to grab more stickers to be ready. All that grabbing makes stickers hard to find, so even more people want them, and it goes round and round.
detail: A gamma squeeze is a self-reinforcing rise in a stock's price driven by the hedging of option dealers. When investors buy many call options, the market makers who sell them usually hedge by buying some of the underlying shares. Gamma measures how fast an option's delta changes, so as the price rises, short-dated out-of-the-money calls gain delta quickly and dealers must buy more shares to stay hedged, which lifts the price further and triggers yet more buying. The effect is strongest when call buying is concentrated in near-expiry contracts on a stock with a small free float. GameStop's surge in January 2021 is widely described as a mix of a short squeeze and a gamma squeeze. The common confusion: a short squeeze is driven by short sellers buying back shares, a gamma squeeze by option hedging. They can happen together, and both usually reverse sharply once the buying stops.
example: Say dealers have sold 10,000 call contracts on XYZ Inc, each covering 100 shares, with a delta of 0.30, so they hold 300,000 shares as a hedge (10,000 × 100 × 0.30). If XYZ rallies and delta climbs to 0.60, the hedge must grow to 600,000 shares, so dealers buy another 300,000 shares into a rising market.
formula: Additional hedge shares ≈ Gamma × Change in share price × Number of contracts × Shares per contract

short: Buying or selling the shares (or other asset) an option is based on, so that small price moves barely change the position's overall value.
kid: If you promise to give a friend a ball later, you keep some balls ready in your bag. When it looks more likely they will want it, you add balls; when less likely, you take some out.
detail: Delta hedging offsets an option's sensitivity to the underlying price, its delta, with an opposite position in the underlying or in futures. A call with a delta of 0.5 gains about ₹0.50 for every ₹1 rise in the share, so someone short that call buys half a share per option to be delta neutral. Because delta changes as the price moves and time passes, the effect measured by gamma, the hedge must be adjusted again and again, which is why it is also called dynamic hedging. Market makers and banks that sell options do this all day, and their buying and selling can calm or amplify market moves. The common confusion: a delta-neutral position is not risk-free. It is still exposed to sudden jumps, changes in implied volatility and time decay, and frequent rebalancing costs money in brokerage and bid-ask spreads.
example: Say a dealer sells call options covering 10,000 shares of ABC Ltd with a delta of 0.40; it buys 4,000 shares (10,000 × 0.40) to be delta neutral. If ABC rises and delta climbs to 0.55, the hedge must grow to 5,500 shares, so the dealer buys 1,500 more.
formula: Hedge shares = −(Option delta × Number of options × Shares per option), counting options sold as negative

short: A rule linking the prices of matching call and put options on the same asset, so that neither can be mispriced without offering riskless profit.
kid: If two different bags always end up holding exactly the same sweets, they should cost the same. If one is cheaper, everyone buys that one until the prices match again.
detail: Put-call parity says that a European call minus a European put, with the same strike and expiry on the same non-dividend-paying asset, equals the asset's price minus the present value of the strike: C − P = S − PV(K). The logic is that a long call plus a short put pays what owning the asset and borrowing the strike amount pays at expiry, so the two must cost the same today. If they drift apart, traders run arbitrage trades called conversions and reversals until prices line up. Parity underpins synthetic positions, explains why a call and a put at the same strike share one implied volatility, and helps check whether an option chain is quoted sensibly. The common confusion: it holds exactly only for European options, the style used on Indian exchanges. For American options, early exercise and dividends turn it into a range rather than an equation.
example: Say ABC Ltd trades at ₹100, a one-year ₹100 call costs ₹12, and the present value of ₹100 payable in a year is ₹95. Parity says the matching put should cost 12 − 100 + 95 = ₹7. If it trades at ₹9 instead, a trader can sell the put, buy the call, short the shares and lend ₹95, locking in ₹2 per share today (9 − 12 + 100 − 95).
formula: C − P = S − PV(K), where PV(K) = K × e^(−rT) (European options, no dividends)

short: Owning a stock and selling someone the right to buy it from you at a set price, earning an upfront fee but capping your gain.
kid: You own a toy car, and a friend gives you a sweet now for the promise that they can buy the car for ten coins later. You keep the sweet either way, but even if the car becomes more special, you only get ten coins.
detail: A covered call combines owning shares with selling (writing) a call option on the same shares, usually at a strike above the current price. The seller collects the premium immediately. If the share stays below the strike, the call expires worthless and the premium is extra income; if it rises above, the shares are called away at the strike, so the upside is capped. Investors use it to earn income on holdings they would be happy to sell at the strike. In India, exchange-traded options come in fixed lots, so you need as many shares as the lot size, and, under the rules as of 2025, stock options are settled by delivery. The common confusion: covered calls are not low-risk income. You keep almost all of the downside if the share falls, cushioned only by the premium, while giving up the big gains.
example: Say you own 100 shares of ABC Ltd (a hypothetical lot size) bought at ₹500 and sell a one-month ₹550 call for ₹10, collecting ₹1,000. If ABC ends at ₹580, your shares go at ₹550 and you make ₹6,000 (₹5,000 on the shares plus the ₹1,000 premium) instead of ₹8,000. If ABC falls to ₹480, the ₹2,000 loss on the shares is cut to ₹1,000 by the premium.
formula: Max profit = (Strike − Purchase price + Premium) × Shares; Breakeven = Purchase price − Premium

short: Buying the right to sell shares you own at a set price, so a big fall costs you only a limited, known amount.
kid: You give a friend one sweet so that, if your toy breaks, they promise to swap it for a good one. If nothing breaks, you have only lost the sweet.
detail: A protective put pairs owning shares with buying a put option on them, usually at a strike slightly below the current price. If the share falls below the strike, gains on the put offset losses on the shares, so the maximum loss is fixed in advance; if it rises, the investor keeps the upside minus the premium paid. It works like insurance: the premium is the cost of cover and the gap down to the strike is the deductible. When the shares and the put are bought together it is called a married put, and fund managers often buy index puts to protect a whole portfolio. The common confusion: 'portfolio insurance' in the 1980s usually meant a dynamic strategy that copied a put by selling futures as markets fell, and that selling is widely blamed for deepening the October 1987 crash. Regular put buying is costly when volatility is high.
example: Say you own 100 shares of ABC Ltd bought at ₹500 and buy a ₹480 put for ₹12, costing ₹1,200. If ABC slumps to ₹400, the shares lose ₹10,000 but the put pays ₹8,000 (₹80 × 100), so your total loss is capped at ₹3,200 (₹10,000 − ₹8,000 + ₹1,200). If ABC rises to ₹600, you gain ₹10,000 on the shares, or ₹8,800 after the premium.
formula: Max loss = (Purchase price − Put strike + Premium) × Shares; Breakeven = Purchase price + Premium

short: Protecting shares you own against a fall by giving up gains above a set level, so their value stays within a chosen range.
kid: You put a soft mat under your block tower so it cannot fall too far, and you agree never to build it taller than the shelf. Your tower stays safely in between.
detail: A collar combines three positions: owning shares, buying an out-of-the-money put to set a floor, and selling an out-of-the-money call to set a ceiling. The premium from the call pays for some or all of the put; when the two premiums match it is called a zero-cost collar. The result is a band: losses below the put strike and gains above the call strike are both cut off. Collars are used by founders and executives with concentrated holdings, by funds protecting past gains, and in currency hedging, where Indian exporters and importers use similar range structures to limit rupee risk. The common confusion: 'zero cost' refers only to the upfront cash. The real cost is the upside you give up, and if the share rallies hard you are obliged to sell at the call strike.
example: Say you own 100 shares of ABC Ltd bought at ₹500, buy a ₹460 put for ₹10 and sell a ₹550 call for ₹10, so the net cost is zero. Whatever happens by expiry, your result stays between a loss of ₹4,000 ((₹500 − ₹460) × 100) and a gain of ₹5,000 ((₹550 − ₹500) × 100).
formula: Net cost = Put premium − Call premium; Floor = Put strike; Ceiling = Call strike

short: Buying both the right to buy and the right to sell at one price and date, profiting if the price moves a lot either way.
kid: You are not sure if tomorrow will be sunny or rainy, so you pack both sunglasses and an umbrella. You only feel clever if the weather turns really wild; on a dull grey day, you carried both for nothing.
detail: A long straddle is the purchase of a call and a put with the same strike, usually at the money, and the same expiry. It profits if the underlying moves far enough in either direction to cover both premiums, so it is a bet on volatility rather than direction. Traders use it ahead of events such as company results, the Union Budget, RBI policy decisions or election results. A short straddle is the reverse: selling both options to collect premium, profiting if the price stays near the strike but facing large, theoretically unlimited losses on a big move; it is popular with Indian index option sellers and needs substantial margin. The common confusion: a big move alone is not enough. After an event, implied volatility often collapses (IV crush), so a straddle bought at high premiums can lose money even when the price moves.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹1,000 before its results, and you buy a ₹1,000 call for ₹40 and a ₹1,000 put for ₹35, paying ₹75. You break even at expiry if ABC is at ₹925 or ₹1,075. If it jumps to ₹1,120, the call is worth ₹120 and you make ₹45 per share; if it ends at ₹1,000, you lose the full ₹75.
formula: Long straddle breakevens = Strike − Total premium and Strike + Total premium

short: Buying the right to buy above today's price and the right to sell below it, which pays off only after a large move either way.
kid: You hang one net high in a tree and lay another low on the grass to catch a bouncing ball. You only catch something if the ball bounces really high or rolls really low.
detail: A long strangle buys an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put with the same expiry but different strikes. Because both options start out of the money, it costs less than a straddle, but the price must move further before it pays. A short strangle sells both options, collecting premium and profiting if the underlying stays between the two strikes; it is one of the most common trades among Indian index option sellers, especially near weekly expiry. Its risk is lopsided: gains are capped at the premium received, while a sudden gap can produce losses many times larger, which is why exchanges demand high margins for it. The common confusion: a strangle uses two different strikes, a straddle one. Traders also underrate how often 'unlikely' moves happen, so a short strangle that wins most weeks can wipe out months of gains in a single session.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹1,000, and you buy a ₹1,050 call for ₹15 and a ₹950 put for ₹12, paying ₹27. You profit at expiry only if ABC ends below ₹923 or above ₹1,077. Anywhere between ₹950 and ₹1,050, both options expire worthless and the ₹27 is lost.
formula: Long strangle breakevens = Put strike − Total premium and Call strike + Total premium

short: A cheaper way to bet on a moderate rise: buy one call and sell another at a higher strike, so profit and loss are capped.
kid: You think your little plant will grow a bit taller, so you make a small bet with a friend. However tall it grows, you can win only a few sweets and lose only a few sweets.
detail: A bull call spread buys a call at a lower strike and sells a call at a higher strike, both with the same expiry. The premium received from the sold call reduces the cost of the bought one, so the trader pays a net debit, which is the maximum loss. In exchange, the profit is capped at the gap between the strikes minus that debit, reached if the price ends at or above the higher strike. It suits a view that the underlying will rise moderately rather than soar. In India it is popular with retail traders because, under exchange margin rules, the hedged structure needs far less margin than selling options outright. The common confusion: 'bull spread' also covers the bull put spread, which is built with puts and collects a credit instead. Both are vertical spreads with a similar payoff shape but different cash flows and margin.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹500. You buy a ₹500 call for ₹20 and sell a ₹540 call for ₹8, paying a net ₹12. At expiry your maximum profit is ₹28 (₹40 − ₹12) if ABC is at ₹540 or above, your maximum loss is ₹12 if it is at ₹500 or below, and you break even at ₹512.
formula: Max profit = (Higher strike − Lower strike) − Net debit; Max loss = Net debit; Breakeven = Lower strike + Net debit

short: A cheaper way to bet on a moderate fall: buy one put and sell another at a lower strike, so profit and loss are capped.
kid: You think your sandcastle will shrink a little when the waves come, so you make a small bet with your brother. However much it shrinks, you can win only a few shells and lose only a few shells.
detail: A bear put spread buys a put at a higher strike and sells a put at a lower strike, both with the same expiry. The premium from the sold put offsets part of the cost of the bought put, leaving a net debit that is the most the trader can lose. The maximum profit is the gap between the strikes minus that debit, earned if the price ends at or below the lower strike. It suits a view that the underlying will fall moderately, and it is cheaper than buying a put outright, especially when implied volatility is high, because the sold put recovers some of the inflated premium. The common confusion: 'bear spread' also includes the bear call spread, which sells a lower-strike call and buys a higher one for a net credit. Both profit from a fall, but their cash flows, margin and behaviour before expiry differ.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹500. You buy a ₹500 put for ₹18 and sell a ₹460 put for ₹6, paying a net ₹12. If ABC ends at ₹460 or lower you make the maximum ₹28 (₹40 − ₹12); at ₹500 or higher you lose ₹12; and you break even at ₹488.
formula: Max profit = (Higher strike − Lower strike) − Net debit; Max loss = Net debit; Breakeven = Higher strike − Net debit

short: Buying one option and selling another of the same type and expiry at a different strike, which caps both the possible gain and loss.
kid: You and a friend agree on a game where you can win at most five marbles and lose at most five marbles. Knowing the limits makes the game feel safer.
detail: A vertical spread combines a bought and a sold option of the same type (both calls or both puts) on the same underlying and expiry but at different strikes; 'vertical' comes from strikes being listed one above another on an option chain. Debit spreads, the bull call spread and bear put spread, cost money upfront and gain if the price moves the right way. Credit spreads, the bull put spread and bear call spread, collect money upfront and gain if the price does not move against the seller. In every case the maximum loss is limited by the gap between the strikes. In India, vertical spreads are widely used because hedged positions need much lower margin than naked option selling under exchange rules. The common confusion: in options, a 'credit spread' is a spread opened for a net credit, unrelated to the credit spread between corporate and government bond yields.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹500 and you open a bull put spread: sell a ₹480 put for ₹10 and buy a ₹460 put for ₹4, collecting ₹6. If ABC stays above ₹480 you keep the ₹6; if it falls below ₹460 you lose the maximum ₹14 (₹20 width − ₹6 credit); breakeven is ₹474.
formula: Width = Higher strike − Lower strike; Debit spread: Max profit = Width − Net debit, Max loss = Net debit; Credit spread: Max profit = Net credit, Max loss = Width − Net credit

short: A four-option trade that earns a set amount if a price stays within a chosen range and has a capped loss if it breaks out.
kid: You bet a friend that your ball will stay inside the playground fence all afternoon. If it does, you win a few sweets; if it flies over, you give some back, but only up to an agreed number.
detail: An iron condor combines a bull put spread below the current price with a bear call spread above it, all four options sharing one expiry. The trader sells an out-of-the-money put and an out-of-the-money call and buys options further out as protection, collecting a net credit. If the underlying ends between the two sold strikes, all the options expire worthless and the credit is kept. If it breaks beyond either protective strike, the loss is capped at the width of that spread minus the credit. It is a bet that the market will stay range-bound and that implied volatility will fall, and it is widely traded on index options. The common confusion: a high win rate is not the same as an edge. The maximum loss is usually several times the maximum gain, so a few large breakouts can erase many small wins.
example: Say an index is at 20,000. You sell a 19,500 put for 60 points and buy a 19,300 put for 30, and sell a 20,500 call for 55 and buy a 20,700 call for 25, collecting 60 points in all. You keep all 60 if the index ends between 19,500 and 20,500; the most you can lose is 140 points (200 − 60); breakevens are 19,440 and 20,560.
formula: Max profit = Net credit; Max loss = Width of the wider wing − Net credit; Breakevens = Sold put strike − Net credit and Sold call strike + Net credit

short: A cheap three-strike options trade that pays most if the price ends exactly at a chosen middle level on expiry, with small, capped losses.
kid: You guess exactly where a rolling marble will stop. If it stops right on your spot you win lots of sweets, near it you win a few, and far away you lose just one sweet.
detail: A long call butterfly buys one call at a lower strike, sells two calls at a middle strike and buys one call at a higher strike, with equal gaps between the strikes and the same expiry; the same shape can be built with puts. It costs a small net debit, which is the maximum loss, and earns the most if the underlying ends exactly at the middle strike, where the profit equals the strike gap minus the debit. It is a low-cost bet that the price will settle near a level. An iron butterfly gets a similar payoff for a net credit by selling an at-the-money call and put and buying out-of-the-money ones as protection. The common confusion: the peak payoff is narrow. With weeks left, a price sitting at the middle strike shows only a small profit. Bond traders also use 'butterfly' for an unrelated yield-curve trade.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹500. You buy a ₹480 call for ₹28, sell two ₹500 calls for ₹15 each and buy a ₹520 call for ₹6, paying a net ₹4. If ABC ends exactly at ₹500 you make ₹16 (₹20 − ₹4); you break even at ₹484 and ₹516; and below ₹480 or above ₹520 you lose just the ₹4.
formula: Long butterfly: Max profit = Strike gap − Net debit; Max loss = Net debit; Breakevens = Lower strike + Net debit and Upper strike − Net debit

short: Selling a near-dated option and buying a later-dated one at the same strike, to profit as the near one loses value faster.
kid: You give away an ice lolly that melts quickly and keep a big block of ice that melts slowly. As long as the room stays cool and calm, you come out ahead.
detail: An options calendar spread sells a short-dated option and buys a longer-dated option of the same type and strike. Short-dated options lose time value fastest, so if the underlying stays near the strike, the sold option decays more quickly than the bought one and the position gains. It also benefits if implied volatility rises, because the longer-dated option is more sensitive to it. It is usually opened for a net debit, which is roughly the maximum loss. If the strikes differ as well as the expiries, it is called a diagonal spread. The common confusion: in Indian futures markets, 'calendar spread' usually means buying one month's futures and selling another's, for example during monthly rollover, which can attract lower margin. That is a different trade from the options version described here.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹1,000. You sell this month's ₹1,000 call for ₹25 and buy next month's ₹1,000 call for ₹40, paying a net ₹15. If ABC is still at ₹1,000 when the near call expires, that call is worthless, and if the longer call is then worth, say, ₹30, your profit is ₹15 (₹30 − ₹15).
formula: Net debit = Far-month option premium − Near-month option premium

short: Selling an option without owning the asset or a protecting option, so the seller faces large and, for calls, unlimited losses.
kid: You promise to sell a friend a toy you do not have for five coins. If that toy suddenly gets very hard to find, you still have to get it somehow, however much it costs.
detail: A naked, or uncovered, option is one sold without an offsetting position. A naked call writer does not own the underlying, so if the price soars the loss has no ceiling; a naked put writer has no protection either, so losses grow all the way down to a price of zero. The seller's reward is only the premium collected, which is why brokers and exchanges demand large margins and may close positions when margin runs short. Many Indian retail traders sell naked index options near expiry because most options expire worthless, but rare gap moves can cause losses far larger than months of premium. A SEBI study published in 2024 found that about 93% of individual F&O traders lost money between FY22 and FY24. The common confusion: naked option selling is different from naked short selling, which means selling shares without having borrowed them.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹550 and you sell a naked ₹600 call for ₹8 on 100 shares, collecting ₹800. If takeover news sends ABC to ₹700 by expiry, the call is worth ₹100, so you lose ₹9,200 ((₹100 − ₹8) × 100), more than eleven times what you collected.
formula: Seller's profit per share: naked call = Premium − max(0, S − K); naked put = Premium − max(0, K − S)

short: A mix of options, and sometimes the asset itself, built to produce the same payoff as a different position, such as owning a share.
kid: You cannot find a toy robot, so you build one from blocks that moves exactly like the real one. It is a different thing, but it does the same job.
detail: A synthetic position recreates the payoff of one instrument using others, relying on put-call parity. The most common is a synthetic long stock or synthetic future: buy a call and sell a put at the same strike and expiry, and the combination gains and loses rupee for rupee with the underlying. Reversing it, selling a call and buying a put, creates a synthetic short. Other combinations copy single options; for example, owning a share plus a put behaves like a call. Traders use synthetics when the real instrument is costly, hard to borrow or heavy on margin, and arbitrageurs compare synthetic and actual futures prices to spot mispricing. The common confusion: synthetic does not mean fake or lower risk. A synthetic long carries the full downside of owning the asset, and its sold put leg needs margin.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹500. You buy a ₹500 call for ₹22 and sell a ₹500 put for ₹18, paying a net ₹4. At expiry you gain ₹56 (₹60 − ₹4) if ABC is at ₹560 and lose ₹54 (₹50 + ₹4) if it is at ₹450, almost exactly as if you had bought the shares; the ₹4 roughly reflects the interest saved by not paying ₹500 upfront.
formula: Synthetic long = Long call + Short put (same strike and expiry); Synthetic short = Short call + Long put

short: Buying the right to buy above today's price while selling the right to sell below it; also a gauge of which direction traders fear more.
kid: If more children pay to be protected from rain than from too much sun, you can tell they are more worried about rain. Comparing the two shows what people fear most.
detail: Risk reversal has two linked meanings. As a strategy, it means buying an out-of-the-money call and selling an out-of-the-money put with the same expiry, often for little or no net cost, which behaves like owning the asset outside the two strikes; the reverse creates a bearish position. As a market measure, mainly in currency options, the 25-delta risk reversal is the implied volatility of a 25-delta call minus that of a 25-delta put. A positive reading means traders pay more for protection against a rise, a negative one against a fall. On equity indices it is usually negative because investors pay up for crash protection. Forex desks, including those quoting dollar-rupee options, watch risk reversals to gauge positioning. The common confusion: a zero-cost risk reversal is not riskless, because the sold put carries the full downside below its strike.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹500, and you buy a ₹530 call for ₹9 and sell a ₹470 put for ₹9, paying nothing net. Above ₹530 you gain like a shareholder, and below ₹470 you lose like one. As a gauge: if a currency pair's 25-delta calls trade at 7.5% implied volatility and its 25-delta puts at 6.0%, the risk reversal is +1.5 volatility points.
formula: 25-delta risk reversal = Implied volatility of 25-delta call − Implied volatility of 25-delta put

short: The price at expiry at which all the options outstanding on an asset would be worth the least in total, so buyers lose the most.
kid: Imagine lots of children made guesses, and a prize must be handed out for every guess that comes true. Max pain is the spot where the fewest prizes have to be given.
detail: Max pain is the strike price at which the total intrinsic value of all open call and put contracts on an underlying would be smallest at expiry, so option buyers as a group lose the most and option writers pay out the least. It is calculated from open interest at each strike, and option chain tools in India show it for the Nifty, Bank Nifty and major stocks. Max pain theory claims prices drift towards this level near expiry because large option writers and hedging flows pull them there. The evidence is weak and mixed: prices can end far from max pain, especially on news, and the level itself shifts as open interest changes during the day. The common confusion: max pain describes open positions; it is not a forecast. Treat it as one input alongside open interest and the put-call ratio, never as a price target.
example: Say a stock's open interest is 200 calls and 800 puts at the ₹95 strike, 500 calls and 600 puts at ₹100, and 900 calls and 100 puts at ₹105, each on one share. Settling at ₹95 would make the options worth ₹4,000 in total (₹5 × 600 + ₹10 × 100), at ₹100 just ₹1,500 (₹5 × 200 + ₹5 × 100), and at ₹105 ₹4,500 (₹10 × 200 + ₹5 × 500). Max pain is therefore ₹100.
formula: Max pain = Strike K that minimises Σ over all strikes Ki of [Call OI(Ki) × max(K − Ki, 0) + Put OI(Ki) × max(Ki − K, 0)]

short: The number of put options traded or open divided by the number of call options, used as a rough gauge of market mood.
kid: Count how many friends brought umbrellas and how many brought sunglasses. If umbrellas win, more people are expecting rain.
detail: The put-call ratio (PCR) divides put activity by call activity on an index or stock. It can be based on trading volume, showing the day's flow, or on open interest, showing positions outstanding; Indian market commentary mostly quotes the open interest PCR for the Nifty and Bank Nifty. A PCR above 1 means more puts than calls. Reading it is tricky. In the US, a high volume PCR is often seen as a sign of fear and therefore contrarian bullish, while Indian analysts often read a rising open interest PCR as bullish because it reflects heavy put writing by sellers betting the market will hold above certain strikes. The common confusion: PCR counts contracts, not who bought and who sold them, so the same number can come from put buyers hedging or put writers selling. Use it with price action, open interest by strike and implied volatility, not alone.
example: Say open interest in an index's options is 1.5 crore put contracts and 1.2 crore call contracts. The put-call ratio is 1.5 ÷ 1.2 = 1.25, meaning 1.25 puts are open for every call.
formula: PCR = Put open interest / Call open interest (or Put volume / Call volume)

short: A table listing every available strike price for an asset's options on a given expiry, showing call and put prices, volume and open positions.
kid: It is like the big menu board at an ice cream shop, listing every flavour and size with its price. One look tells you what is on offer and what most people are choosing.
detail: An option chain is the standard display of all option contracts on one underlying for a chosen expiry. Strikes run down the middle, with calls usually on the left and puts on the right. For each contract it shows the last traded price, bid and ask, volume, open interest, change in open interest and often implied volatility and Greeks. Strikes near the current price are at the money, and the chain is usually shaded to mark in-the-money options. The NSE publishes free option chains for indices and F&O stocks, and broker apps build trading screens around them. Traders use it to judge liquidity, spot strikes with heavy open interest that may act as support or resistance, and work out the put-call ratio and max pain. The common confusion: the last traded price on an illiquid strike may be stale, so check the bid-ask spread before trading.
example: Say ABC Ltd trades at ₹502. On its option chain the ₹500 row shows a call at ₹18 and a put at ₹14. The call is ₹2 in the money, so ₹16 of its price is time value, while the put is out of the money, so all ₹14 of its price is time value.

short: Contracts giving the right to gain from a rise or fall in a stock market index, such as the Nifty 50, settled in cash.
kid: Instead of betting on one runner, you bet on how fast the whole team runs on average. At the end you get sweets, not runners.
detail: Index options are call and put options on a stock index rather than a single share. In India the main contracts are on the Nifty 50, Bank Nifty and Sensex; globally, S&P 500 options dominate. Indian index options are European style, so they can be exercised only at expiry, and they are cash settled: the difference between the settlement level and the strike, times the lot size, is paid in rupees. They drive most of the trading that has made the NSE the world's largest derivatives exchange by contracts traded in recent years. Concerned by heavy retail losses, SEBI tightened the rules from late 2024; under the rules as of 2025, minimum contract sizes are higher, each exchange offers one weekly expiry and option premiums are collected upfront. The common confusion: headline turnover figures are usually notional values, many times larger than the premiums actually paid.
example: Say an index is at 20,000 and you buy a 20,200 call for 100 points with a hypothetical lot size of 75, paying ₹7,500. If the index settles at 20,500 on expiry, the call is worth 300 points, so you receive ₹22,500 in cash, a profit of ₹15,000, and no shares change hands.
formula: Cash settlement of a call = max(0, Settlement index level − Strike) × Lot size

short: Exchange-traded contracts giving the right to buy or sell a particular company's shares at a set price on or before a set date.
kid: You give a friend a sweet so that you may buy their toy car for ten coins next week if you still want it. If you change your mind, you just lose the sweet.
detail: Stock options are calls and puts on individual listed shares. In India they are available only on stocks admitted to the F&O segment, a list of roughly two hundred larger, liquid companies as of 2025 that is revised periodically. Indian stock options are European style and, since 2019 under SEBI rules, physically settled: an in-the-money option held to expiry leads to actual delivery of shares, so a call buyer must pay the full value and the seller must deliver. Under the rules as of 2025, they have monthly expiries only. Investors use them to hedge holdings, earn income through covered calls or take a view on company results. The common confusion: exchange-traded stock options are different from employee stock options (ESOPs), which a company grants its staff as pay, cannot be traded and usually vest over years. News about a chief executive's 'stock options' almost always means the latter.
example: Say you buy a ₹1,000 call on ABC Ltd for ₹30 with a lot of 500 shares, paying ₹15,000. If ABC is at ₹1,080 at expiry and you hold the call, physical settlement means you pay ₹5 lakh (₹1,000 × 500) and receive 500 shares worth ₹5.4 lakh, a net gain of ₹25,000 after the premium.

short: Option contracts that run out every week instead of every month, and the trading day on which they end.
kid: Some coupons work for a whole month, but these ones stop working at the end of each week. On the last day, people rush to use them before they become worthless.
detail: Weekly options are contracts that expire every week, giving traders cheap, short-dated exposure; the session on which they expire is called expiry day. With so little time left, their premiums are small and swing sharply, and Indian expiry days have seen some of the highest options volumes in the world. Concerned by retail losses, SEBI limited each exchange to weekly options on a single benchmark index from November 2024, so the NSE kept Nifty 50 weeklies and the BSE kept Sensex weeklies, while Bank Nifty and other weeklies were discontinued. Under the rules as of 2025, NSE weeklies expire on Tuesdays and BSE weeklies on Thursdays; other index and stock options expire monthly. In the US, S&P 500 options now expire every weekday. The common confusion: a cheap weekly option is not a low-risk bet. Time decay is fastest in the final days, so most out-of-the-money weeklies expire worthless.
example: Say an at-the-money weekly index call costs 120 points five days before expiry. If the index ends the week exactly where it started, the call expires worthless and the buyer loses all 120 points, which is ₹9,000 on a hypothetical lot of 75.

short: Options bought or sold on the same day they expire, so the whole bet plays out within a few hours.
kid: It is like buying a ticket for a race that ends in a few minutes. You find out very quickly whether you win a prize or nothing at all.
detail: Zero-days-to-expiry (0DTE) options are contracts traded on their final day, with hours rather than weeks of life left. Having almost no time value, their prices react violently to small moves: a contract can multiply in value or fall to zero within minutes. In the US, Cboe added Tuesday and Thursday expiries for S&P 500 options in 2022, so these options now expire every weekday, and same-day contracts have since grown into a large share of S&P 500 option volume. In India, contracts traded on weekly expiry day are effectively 0DTE options and account for much of the boom in index option volumes. Some analysts worry that heavy 0DTE trading, and the hedging by dealers on the other side, can amplify intraday swings. The common confusion: a tiny premium does not mean small risk for sellers, who can face large losses from one sharp move in the final hours.
example: Say an index is at 5,000 and a trader pays $2 for a same-day 5,010 call with a multiplier of 100, or $200 in all. If the index closes at 5,030, the call is worth $20, or $2,000, a profit of $1,800; if it closes at 5,005, the call expires worthless and the $200 is lost.

short: Exchange-traded options with more than a year until expiry, letting investors take a long-term view on a stock or index for a smaller upfront sum.
kid: Most promises with friends last a week, but this one lasts for two whole birthdays. You pay a little now to keep your choice open for a long time.
detail: LEAPS, short for Long-Term Equity AnticiPation Securities, are listed options with expiries of more than one year, typically up to about three years; the name is a Cboe trademark, and similar long-dated options exist on other exchanges. They work like ordinary calls and puts but carry much more time value, so they cost more, lose value slowly at first and are sensitive to interest rates and implied volatility. Investors buy long-dated calls as a cheaper, leveraged substitute for owning shares, or long-dated puts as multi-year protection. In India, trading is concentrated in near-dated contracts; the NSE does list longer-dated Nifty options, but they trade thinly. The common confusion: a LEAPS call is not the same as owning the stock. It earns no dividends, carries no voting rights and can expire worthless if the share merely goes nowhere for two years.
example: Say XYZ Inc trades at $100 and a two-year $100 call costs $18, so controlling 100 shares costs $1,800 instead of $10,000. If XYZ is at $140 at expiry, the call is worth $4,000, a profit of $2,200, or about 122% of the outlay, versus $4,000, or 40%, from owning the shares; if XYZ ends at $100 or lower, the whole $1,800 is lost.

short: Any option with non-standard features, such as a payoff based on an average price or one that switches off if a level is touched.
kid: A normal game has simple rules, but some games add special twists, like 'if you ever step on the red tile, you are out'. Some promises come with special twists like that too.
detail: An exotic option is any option whose terms go beyond a plain, or vanilla, call or put. Common types include barrier options, which come alive (knock-in) or die (knock-out) if the price touches a set level; Asian options, whose payoff depends on the average price over a period; lookback options, based on the best price reached; and digital options with a fixed payout. Most are sold over the counter by banks to companies and wealthy clients, tailored to a specific need, and they are often cheaper than vanilla options because of the extra conditions. They are harder to value, and buyers may not fully grasp the risks. Around 2008, many Indian exporters suffered heavy losses on complex currency option structures sold by banks, leading to disputes and tighter RBI rules. The common confusion: 'exotic' does not mean rare or illegal; Asian options, for example, are standard in commodity hedging.
example: Say a bank offers a one-year knock-out call on a hypothetical index at 1,000, with a strike of 1,000 and a barrier at 1,200, for ₹30 instead of ₹50 for a plain call. If the index ends at 1,150 without ever touching 1,200, it pays ₹150; but if the index touches 1,200 even once, the option dies and pays nothing, even if the index ends at 1,190.

short: A bet-like contract that pays a fixed amount if a condition is met, such as a price ending above a level, and nothing otherwise.
kid: You guess whether it will rain tomorrow. If you are right, you get exactly one big sweet; if you are wrong, you get nothing at all.
detail: A binary, or digital, option has an all-or-nothing payoff: a fixed sum if the underlying ends above (or below) the strike at expiry, otherwise zero. Its price, as a share of the payout, roughly reflects the market's estimated probability of finishing in the money. Banks use digital features inside structured products, and some regulated exchanges list binary-style contracts. However, most binary options marketed online to retail traders are short-dated bets on currency or crypto prices offered by unregulated platforms, with odds tilted against customers and often fraud. The EU's securities regulator banned their sale to retail investors in 2018. In India, the RBI keeps an Alert List of unauthorised forex trading platforms, and residents may deal in forex only with authorised entities, on recognised exchanges or RBI-authorised platforms. The common confusion: a binary option is not a normal option with a small premium; its payout never exceeds the fixed amount.
example: Say a binary option pays ₹100 if ABC Ltd closes above ₹500 on Friday and nothing otherwise, and it costs ₹40. If ABC closes at ₹501 you receive ₹100, a profit of ₹60; at ₹499 you receive nothing and lose ₹40. The ₹40 price implies the market sees roughly a 40% chance of a close above ₹500.
formula: Price of a cash-or-nothing call ≈ Payout × e^(−rT) × N(d2), where N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money

short: An index, run by the Cboe exchange in Chicago, that measures how much movement traders expect in the S&P 500 over the next 30 days.
kid: When grown-ups are nervous about a stormy week, they pay more for umbrellas. This number counts how much they are paying, so a big number means lots of worry.
detail: The Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX, estimates the annualised volatility of the S&P 500 expected over the next 30 days, derived from the prices of a wide range of S&P 500 index options. Introduced in 1993 and redesigned in 2003, it rises when investors pay up for options, especially puts for protection, so it usually jumps when stocks fall; hence the nickname 'fear gauge'. A VIX of 20 implies an expected annual move of about 20%, or roughly 5.8% over a month. Its record closing high, about 82.7, came in March 2020. VIX futures and options let investors trade volatility directly. India's equivalent, India VIX, is calculated by the NSE from Nifty options. The common confusion: VIX measures the expected size of moves in either direction, not whether markets will rise or fall, and it cannot be bought directly; VIX-linked products track futures and can lose value steadily over time.
example: Say the VIX is at 20 and the S&P 500 is at a hypothetical 5,000. Dividing 20 by the square root of 12 (about 3.46) gives an expected one-month move of about 5.8%, so options are pricing a typical range of roughly ±290 points over the next 30 days.
formula: VIX = 100 × √σ², where σ² = (2/T) × Σ (ΔKi / Ki²) × e^(RT) × Q(Ki) − (1/T) × (F/K0 − 1)², computed for two expiries and interpolated to 30 days; expected 30-day move ≈ VIX / √12

short: Earning an upfront fee by promising to buy shares at a set price if asked, while keeping enough cash aside to honour that promise.
kid: A friend gives you a sweet now, and you promise to buy their teddy for ten coins next week if they want to sell it. You keep ten coins safe in your piggy bank, just in case.
detail: A cash-secured put is the sale of a put option backed by cash equal to the strike price times the number of shares. The seller collects the premium upfront. If the share stays above the strike, the put expires worthless and the premium is kept; if it falls below, the seller must buy the shares at the strike, effectively at the strike minus the premium. Investors use it to get paid while waiting to buy a stock they like at a lower price, and its payoff mirrors a covered call, as put-call parity implies. In Indian market commentary, heavy put writing at a strike is often read as traders expecting support there. The common confusion: 'cash-secured' means the cash is there, not that the trade is safe. If the share collapses, the seller still buys at the strike and bears the full fall, cushioned only by the premium.
example: Say ABC Ltd is at ₹520 and you sell a ₹500 put on 100 shares for ₹12, collecting ₹1,200 and setting aside ₹50,000. If ABC stays above ₹500, you keep ₹1,200, a 2.4% return on the cash. If ABC ends at ₹460, you buy at ₹500, an effective cost of ₹488 after the premium, and sit on a paper loss of ₹2,800 ((₹488 − ₹460) × 100).
formula: Cash set aside = Strike × Shares; Max profit = Premium; Breakeven = Strike − Premium

short: An estimate of how much option dealers must buy or sell of a stock or index as prices move, which can calm or amplify swings.
kid: Some helpers on a seesaw push down when it goes up and push up when it goes down, keeping it steady. Other helpers push the same way it is already going, making it swing wildly.
detail: Dealer gamma exposure (GEX) estimates the net gamma held by options market makers across all strikes of an index or stock, expressed as the value of the underlying they would need to trade for each 1% move to stay delta hedged. When dealers are net long gamma (positive gamma), hedging makes them sell into rallies and buy into dips, which tends to dampen volatility and can pin prices near large strikes. When they are net short gamma (negative gamma), they must buy as prices rise and sell as they fall, which can accelerate moves, as in gamma squeezes and sharp sell-offs. Analysts estimate GEX from open interest by assuming which side dealers are on, often that customers buy puts and sell calls. The common confusion: GEX is a model output, not reported data. Its assumptions can be wrong, and the figure shifts as options expire, especially around large expiries.
example: Say dealers in XYZ Inc options hold net gamma of +50,000 shares per $1 move. If XYZ rises $2, their delta grows by 100,000 shares, so to stay hedged they sell 100,000 shares into the rally; with gamma of −50,000, they would instead have to buy 100,000 shares, pushing the price further up.
formula: GEX per 1% move = Σ (Gamma × Open interest × Contract multiplier × Spot price² × 0.01), with call gamma counted positive and put gamma negative under the usual dealer-positioning assumption
